subject: Physical Education
name: Physical Education, Units 1 and 2
about: VCE, The body in motion, and sport in society
syllabus: VCE Physical Education Study Design (from 2025), Units 1 and 2

units.title: Unit 1: The human body in motion

points.title: Functions of the skeleton
points.brief: The skeleton supports the body, protects organs, allows movement through levers, stores minerals and makes blood cells.

points.title: Types of bones
points.brief: Long, short, flat, irregular and sesamoid bones each suit a job, such as long bones for leverage.

points.title: Types of joints
points.brief: Joints are fibrous (no movement), cartilaginous (slight movement) or synovial (free movement).

points.title: Synovial joints
points.brief: Freely moving joints, such as the knee and shoulder, with cartilage, synovial fluid and ligaments that allow and protect movement.

points.title: Movement terms
points.brief: Flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation and circumduction describe how body parts move at joints.

points.title: Major muscles
points.brief: The main muscles of the body, such as the quadriceps, hamstrings, deltoids and biceps, and the movements each produces.

points.title: Agonists, antagonists and stabilisers
points.brief: The agonist causes a movement, the antagonist relaxes to allow it, and stabilisers hold other joints steady.

points.title: Types of muscle contraction
points.brief: Concentric contractions shorten the muscle, eccentric ones lengthen it under load, and isometric ones hold it still.

points.title: Muscle fibre types
points.brief: Slow-twitch fibres resist fatigue and suit endurance; fast-twitch fibres are powerful but tire quickly. Fibre arrangement also affects force.

points.title: Motor units
points.brief: A nerve and the fibres it controls form a motor unit. Small units are recruited first, and each unit contracts fully or not at all.

points.title: Levers in the body
points.brief: Bones act as levers, joints as axes and muscles as the force, producing movement in lever systems.

points.title: Musculoskeletal injuries
points.brief: Acute injuries such as sprains happen suddenly; chronic problems such as overtraining syndrome, arthritis and osteoporosis develop over time.

points.title: Preventing injury
points.brief: Warming up, cooling down and proper rehabilitation help prevent injury or stop it coming back.

points.title: Physical aids
points.brief: Protective equipment, taping and braces support joints and muscles and reduce the risk of injury.

points.title: Structure of the heart
points.brief: The heart has four chambers, two atria and two ventricles, with valves that keep blood flowing one way.

points.title: Blood vessels
points.brief: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins return it, and capillaries let gases and nutrients pass to tissues.

points.title: Components of blood
points.brief: Red blood cells carry oxygen, white cells fight infection, platelets help clotting, and plasma carries nutrients and wastes.

points.title: Heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output
points.brief: Cardiac output is the blood pumped each minute, equal to heart rate times stroke volume.

points.title: Blood flow at rest and in exercise
points.brief: During exercise, more blood goes to working muscles and less to organs such as the gut, as the heart pumps harder.

points.title: Thermoregulation
points.brief: Blood vessels widen near the skin to lose heat and narrow to keep it, controlling body temperature at rest and in exercise.

points.title: The respiratory system
points.brief: Air passes through the nose, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli, where gas exchange happens.

points.title: Ventilation
points.brief: Ventilation is the air breathed each minute, equal to breathing rate times the volume of each breath.

points.title: Gas exchange
points.brief: Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between the alveoli and capillaries in the lungs, and between capillaries and muscles.

points.title: Benefits of regular aerobic exercise
points.brief: Regular aerobic exercise strengthens the heart and lungs so they deliver more oxygen to the body.

points.title: Substances that boost performance
points.brief: Substances such as anabolic steroids build muscle but carry health risks and are banned in sport.

points.title: Boosting the cardiorespiratory system
points.brief: Altitude training is allowed; EPO, blood doping and beta blockers are banned. Each has benefits and health risks.

points.title: Ethics of boosting performance
points.brief: Using banned substances and methods raises questions of fairness, health, the spirit of sport and pressure on athletes.

units.title: Unit 2: Physical activity, sport, exercise and society

points.title: Physical activity, exercise and sport
points.brief: Physical activity includes play, games, formal and informal sport, active transport, chores, exercise and recreation.

points.title: Sedentary behaviour
points.brief: Time spent sitting or lying while awake, such as screen time, which harms health even in people who exercise.

points.title: Physical activity guidelines
points.brief: Australia's guidelines set how much activity each age group needs, such as 60 minutes a day for young people, and to limit sitting.

points.title: Benefits of physical activity
points.brief: Regular activity has physical, social, mental, emotional and spiritual benefits.

points.title: Activity levels and trends
points.brief: Data shows how many Australians meet the guidelines, how activity changes with age and how sedentary behaviour is rising.

points.title: Measuring physical activity
points.brief: Activity can be measured with questionnaires, diaries, pedometers, accelerometers and heart rate monitors, each with strengths and limits.

points.title: The social-ecological model
points.brief: A model showing activity is shaped at several levels, the individual, social, physical environment and policy.

points.title: Barriers and enablers to activity
points.brief: Gender, family, peers, income, community and cultural norms can make it easier or harder for a person to be active.

points.title: Population-wide initiatives
points.brief: Programs, policies and environments, such as bike paths or school sport, aim to get whole populations moving.

points.title: A personal activity plan
points.brief: A plan built around a person's goals, with self-management skills such as goal setting and self-monitoring, to be more active and sit less.

points.title: Health-related fitness
points.brief: Aerobic power, muscular strength and endurance and flexibility affect health, and each depends on factors such as age, sex and training.

points.title: Functional movement assessment
points.brief: Testing how well a person moves, weighing physical, psychological and sociocultural factors before they start a program.

points.title: Screening and informed consent
points.brief: Health screening before activity finds risks, and informed consent means the person understands and agrees to the testing.

points.title: Reliable and valid assessment
points.brief: A reliable test gives the same result each time, a valid test measures what it should, and an accurate one is close to the true value.

points.title: Hormones and physical activity
points.brief: Hormonal changes, such as the menstrual cycle, can be considered when planning training and activity.

points.title: Injury, concussion and safety
points.brief: Concussion and knee injuries are common in sport, and rules, equipment and return-to-play protocols manage the risk.

points.title: Psychological skills and sleep
points.brief: Strategies for confidence, focus and good sleep support performance and enjoyment of sport.

points.title: Mental fitness in sport
points.brief: Physical activity supports mental fitness, and elite sport pathways have a duty to protect athletes' mental health.

chapters.title: Interpersonal and structural issues in sport

points.title: Living in the city or the country
points.brief: Distance, facilities, cost and choice of sports differ between rural and urban areas, affecting who can play.

points.title: Coaching
points.brief: Coaching styles, good program design and ethical behaviour, including keeping young athletes safe, shape participation and performance.

points.title: Technology in sport
points.brief: Equipment, data and video review can improve performance and fairness, but raise questions about cost and advantage.

points.title: Media and sport
points.brief: The media shapes which sports are popular, how athletes are seen and how sport is funded.

points.title: Inclusion in sport
points.brief: Policies and clubs can include Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, people from diverse cultures, people with disability and gender-diverse people.

points.title: Gender equity in sport
points.brief: Gaps in pay, media coverage and the number of women coaching and running sport show where gender equity is still lacking.
